articles.title: GSAP vs a Motion Runtime: Why 'Which Is Better' Is the Wrong Question
articles.excerpt: Every comparison post about GSAP starts the same way: a table with checkmarks, where the author's tool has all of them. Let me try a more useful framing. GSAP is a library you call. Exode is an enviro…
articles.body: Every comparison post about GSAP starts the same way: a table with checkmarks, where the author's tool has all of them. Let me try a more useful framing. GSAP is a library you call. Exode is an environment that writes code which calls things. Those are different rungs of the stack. You can use both. You cannot meaningfully replace one with the other, and most teams that try end up with a worse version of what they had. What GSAP gets right that nobody should argue with I have shipped GSAP in production for years. It is fast, it is stable, and the timeline API is still the best mental model for sequencing in JavaScript: const tl = gsap . timeline ( { defaults : { ease : "power3.out" } } ) ; tl . from ( ".card" , { y : 24 , opacity : 0 , stagger : 0.06 } ) .

articles.title: From Chat to Deliverables: How to Design Reliable AI Workflows
articles.excerpt: The Limitation of Pure Conversational AI In modern knowledge work, relying solely on conversational prompts—such as "draft an industry analysis report" or "prepare a project plan"—frequently falls sho…
articles.body: The Limitation of Pure Conversational AI In modern knowledge work, relying solely on conversational prompts—such as "draft an industry analysis report" or "prepare a project plan"—frequently falls short of business standards. Chat-based interfaces introduce specific bottlenecks when tasked with producing formal deliverables: Context Decay and Drift : Linear chat conversations emphasize open-ended dialogue. As context expands across multiple turns, models often lose track of initial constraints, resulting in outputs that diverge from the original outline. Absence of Tool Execution and File Creation : Standard chat models output text blocks into conversation bubbles. They do not natively orchestrate tools, execute file-system operations, or structure output into production-ready documents.

articles.title: Next.js Server Action Presigned Uploads — Private Storage, Browser Direct and Signed URLs
articles.excerpt: Short answer: for a marketplace that serves private reports, let a Next.js server action mint a short-lived presigned upload URL, send the browser straight to a private bucket, and mint a separate sig…
articles.body: Short answer: for a marketplace that serves private reports, let a Next.js server action mint a short-lived presigned upload URL, send the browser straight to a private bucket, and mint a separate signed read URL when the customer downloads. Pick the storage backend by testing tenant isolation, not by counting SDK methods. The request path is small: browser asks your app for an upload session; the app authenticates the customer, chooses a key under that tenant, and asks storage to presign it; the browser uploads the File without streaming bytes through Next.js. Later, your app checks its database record and issues a short-lived read link. The bucket stays private.

articles.body: Learning to code is a continuous journey, and I believe one of the best ways to strengthen programming concepts is to put them into practice. Today, I built a small JavaScript project called Wildlife Tracker as part of my ongoing learning journey. The goal was to practise working with JavaScript objects and understand how their properties can be accessed, added, updated, and deleted. Let's explore what I practised! Creating JavaScript Objects I started by creating two objects representing different animals: a tiger and an elephant. Each object contains three properties: species: Represents the animal's name. age: Stores the animal's age. isEndangered: Indicates whether the animal is endangered.

articles.title: Retrieval Architecture for Changelog Trackers — Ranking Signals for Migration
articles.excerpt: Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to a changelog entry. Keep the ranking contract in your application so swappin…
articles.body: Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to a changelog entry. Keep the ranking contract in your application so swapping a search or vector provider does not force a rewrite. That sounds abstract until a tracker answers “what changed in the checkout API?” with a paragraph from the wrong release. For an e-commerce changelog tracker, grounding is the product feature: every sentence needs a release, URL, and section anchor. Ranking signals should make that evidence easier to select, not hide it behind a single similarity score. Start with a retrieval contract, not a vendor I write the answer shape first. A result has document_id , chunk_id , release_date , source_url , section , and a short text excerpt.

articles.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
articles.excerpt: Voyager 1 just reached a light-day in space, but Voyager 2 won't do the same until 2035, due to speed choices made throughout their 50-year missions.
articles.body: Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer?

articles.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
articles.excerpt: The British company Foundational thinks its laser-reflecting tech can help humanity fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test.
articles.body: A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors.

articles.title: NASA to Cover 35th SpaceX Resupply Mission Space Station Departure
articles.excerpt: NASA and its international partners are set to receive scientific research samples and hardware as a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft departs the International Space Station no earlier than Wednesday, Nov. 18…
articles.body: A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft supporting the company’s 34th commercial resupply services mission for NASA departs the International Space Station following its undocking from the Harmony module’s forward port. Credit: NASA/Jessica Meir NASA and its international partners are set to receive scientific research samples and hardware as a SpaceX Dragon spacecraft departs the International Space Station no earlier than Wednesday, Nov. 18, for its return to Earth. Pending weather conditions, the Dragon spacecraft will undock from the Harmony module’s space-facing port at 11:05 a.m. EST, following a command sent by ground controllers at SpaceX’s facility in Hawthorne, California.

articles.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
articles.excerpt: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova.
articles.body: Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth.
